newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fear of war in Zaire capital spurs moves for talks.
newsitem.headline: Fear of war in Zaire capital spurs moves for talks.

text.p: As rebels target Kinshasa, concern is growing over the prospect of bloodshed and anarchy in Zaire's sprawling capital, diplomats in the city say.

South Africa on Tuesday predicted dramatic progress within days in ending the civil war to avert mayhem in Kinshasa, a city of over five million people which is the last remaining stronghold of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
But after two days of anti-Mobutu protests which brought the city to a standstill, many residents are asking what happens if Laurent Kabila's rebels reach town.
"The Americans, the French and other big powers have all made contingency plans to rescue their people, but what happens to the rest of us?," a worried African diplomat said.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have stationed a total of more than 1,000 military personnel in the nearby Congolese capital Brazzaville.
The U.S. carrier Nassau is off Zaire's small coastline to the west, close to Angola, with additional personnel.
Regular exercises by the Western forces in recent days, including on the river Zaire that separates Brazzaville and Kinshasa, have added to a growing sense of fear in Kinshasa.
"Planes leaving Kinshasa in recent weeks have been packed with dependants of foreigners or well-off Zaireans," an airline worker at Kinshasa international airport told Reuters.

"People don't want to take any chances. The experience in Liberia shows a lot of damage could be done before foreign forces extend their rescue mission to cover non-Westerners," said the African diplomat who asked not to be named.
The United States mounted a military operation to rescue its citizens and other foreigners when militia warfare exploded in the Liberian capital Monrovia in April and May, 1995.

Kabila's rebels who have seized more than a half of Zaire since taking up arms to topple Mobutu in October, resumed their whirlwind drive on Monday, after a three-day pause to allow Mobutu time to step down.
The rebels say they are now 300 km (180 miles) from Kinshasa, a claim ridiculed by the Zaire government and questioned by independent military analysts.

But given the inability of Zaire's notoriously undisciplined army to offer resistance to the rebels, many Zaireans have no reason to believe government forces will be any more capable of holding onto Kinshasa.

The United States on Monday expressed the strongest concern over the fate of Kinshasa. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a briefing it would be a "crime and a terrible tragedy" if war reached the capital.

Kabila insists on direct talks with Mobutu to negotiate an end to Mobutu's 32-year rule. In its statements on preparations for a new round of talks on Zaire, South Africa stopped short of announcing if the two men would be involved.
"We are in constant touch with all the major role players in Zaire," Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo told parliament.
"International efforts will see some dramatic progress within the next few days," Nzo said without elaborating.
Earlier Nzo's deputy Aziz Pahad told a parliamentary committee that South Africa would accelerate efforts to facilitate talks between Kabila and Mobutu. REUTER
